3. NDPC AT A GLANCE
4
3.1 Establishment of the Commission
The Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) was established under the
Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 as the independent Data Protection Authority
which superintends over all matters relating to personal data protection in
Nigeria. NDPC is the successor of the Nigeria Data Protection Bureau (NDPB)
which was established on the 4th of February, 2022 to implement the Nigeria
Data Protection Regulation (NDPR), 2019.
3.2 Enabling Act
Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDPA) came into force on the 12th of June,
2023 (Nigeria’s Democracy Day) after presidential assent by His Excellency,
President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR.
3.3 Our Mission
We are committed towards making
data privacy a cornerstone of
sustainable digital economy in
Nigeria.
3.4 Our Vision
To be a resilient world class institution
for the protection of data privacy.
3.5 Our Values
Accountability, Integrity, Fairness and
Transparency.
3.6 Our Motto
Championing Privacy Rights.

3.8 Nigeria Data Protection Strategic Roadmap
and Action Plan (NDP-SRAP) 2023-2027 Pillars
• Governance 7
This pillar addresses the regulatory powers of the Commission through
actions and initiatives on the enabling law on data protection, regulation
of the data processing activities of data controllers and data processors,
enforcement of data-subjects rights and remediation of data privacy and
protection breaches. It comprises the following sub-pillars: Legal, Policy,
Administrative, Risk Management and Regulatory Framework.
• Human Capital Development
This pillar addresses knowledge gaps through turn-key solutions. We
are cognizant of the imperatives of data governance know-how in the
evolving 4th Industrial Revolution and its implication for sustainable
development (health, education, security, economy, environment, etc) in
emerging economies. Thus, among other initiatives, we have put in place
a comprehensive process of in-country training and certification on data
privacy and protection.
• Ecosystem and Technology
Through a broad spectrum of initiatives, this pillar focuses on the impact
of ecosystem and technology on privacy. We are desirous of creating a
balance between fundamental rights and freedoms vis-à-vis the legitimate
targets of business development. Industry, Infrastructure and Disruptive
Innovation are the sub-pillars under Ecosystem and Technology.
• Cooperation and Collaboration
The pillar takes into consideration the dynamics of the multivalent nature
of the modern society and the interdependence of lives and livelihoods.
These factors are crucial to cross-border data flows and the exchange of
goods and services across borders. Therefore, we are creating consensus
building channels and effective platforms through which well-meaning
stakeholders can work together in developing an inclusive digital economy.
• Funding and Sustainability
The goal is to evolve a trusted and sustainable ecosystem with regulations
that ensure stability (predictability not stagnation), and equity that grows
and deepens the data privacy ecosystem in a way that does not burden
the data subjects.

4.2 Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDPA), 2023.
The signing of the Nigeria Data Bill into law on the 12th of June, 2023 is arguably
one of the historic milestones of the current administration of His Excellency,
14
President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR. In drafting the Bill, the Commission
worked with the Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital
Economy, The Federal Ministry of Justice, and International Development
Institutions (World Bank, European Investment Bank and French Development
Agency) through the Nigeria Digital Identity for Development Project Office
(ID4D).
The Act comprises 12 parts, namely:
i. Objectives and Application
ii. Establishment of the Nigeria Data Protection Commission, and Its
Governing Council
iii. Appointment of the National Commissioner, and other Staff of the
Commission
iv. Financial Provisions
v. Principles and Lawful Basis Governing Processing of Personal Data
vi. Rights of a Data Subject
vii. Data Security
viii. Cross-Border Transfers of Personal Data
ix. Registration and Fees
x. Enforcement
xi. Legal Proceedings
xii. Miscellaneous Provisions
The Act established the Nigeria Data Protection Commission as the
independent data protection authority in Nigeria and invested it with powers
to superintend over all personal data processing in Nigeria. To ensure the
constitutional primacy of fundamental rights, the Act provides under section
63 thus:
Where the provisions of any other law or
enactment, in so far as they provide or relate
directly or indirectly to the processing of
personal data, are inconsistent with any of
the provisions of this Act, the provisions of
this Act shall prevail.

4.3 NDPA Compliance Audit Returns
Compliance Audit Returns is a potent tool of accountability. The Audit
parameters cover:
15
• Governance
• Data Protection Officers and Data Protection Compliance Organizations
• Documentation to Demonstrate Compliance
• Data Processing Activities
In the year 2023, the Commission has recorded 1674 Audit filings. The
Commission is developing a new audit process which will be automated
thereby providing an opportunity for large-scale evaluation of compliance audit
processes. A Guidance Notice on the Filing of Data Protection Compliance
Audit Returns (CAR) for 2022 (NDPC/HQ/GN/VOL.01/23) has been issued. It
contains metrics of accountability being used by the Commission for National
Data Protection Adequacy Programme Whitelist.
4.4 Complaints and Investigation
The Commission pays close attention to complaints and investigations in line
with provisions of Part 10 of the NDPA which deals with Enforcement. As a new
Data Protection Authority, the Commission initiated Pre-Action Conferences
to investigate complaints of privacy breaches which may have seismic effects
on the data processing ecosystem in Nigeria. Investigations include:
• Possibility of breach of data subjects’ right to rectification
• Possibility of data manipulation and privacy breaches
• Effective Technical and Organisational Measures to prevent data
security breaches
• Allegation of privacy breaches on social media platforms
• Transparency of data controllers and processors
4.5 NDPA General Application and
Implementation Directive (GAID)
The central objective is to provide guidance in the following areas inter alia:
a. Objectives and Application of the Act

4.6 Code of Conduct for Data Protection
Compliance Organizations (DPCOs)
The Commission prioritizes professional standards and duty of care among
DPCOs because of the strategic role they play in developing a culture of
compliance in the data processing ecosystem. The Commission has registered
more DPCOs bringing the number to 163. The services being offered by DPCOs
include but are not limited to the following:
a. Data Protection Compliance Audit
b. Training
c. Vetting Data Processing Agreements
d. Drafting of Privacy Policy
e. Interfacing with the Commission on behalf of Data Controllers and Data
Processors
f. Providing Industry Insights
The objectives of the Code of Conduct are to:
a. Promote professionalism in compliance service delivery within the Data
Protection and Privacy ecosystem
b. Ensure fundamental uniformity in compliance processes under extant
regulatory framework for data processing
c. Encourage the adoption of data ethics as a guiding principle in data
protection compliance services
d. Foster discipline and uphold accountability among DPCOs
e. Prescribe fundamental standards in continuous capacity building and
awareness creation services which may be carried out by DPCOs
f. Encourage Corporate Social Responsibility for the advancement of Data
Protection and Privacy in Nigeria
g. Foster trust in the data governance processes of Nigeria’s digital
economy

Nigeria Data Protection Annual Report 2023
4.7 Strategic Knowledge Exchange and
International Regulators’ Networking
The Commission accords priority to bilateral and multilateral cooperation 17
because of the globally interconnected nature of data processing platforms.
Nigerians are data subjects to many data controllers and data processors in
foreign jurisdictions. Meta alone has over 40 million subscribers in Nigeria.
There are approximately over 100 million internet users in Nigeria – making
the personal data of Nigerians accessible anywhere in the world. The only
effective way of ensuring data privacy rights, national security, development
of the local digital economy and the overall data sovereignty of Nigeria is
through bilateral cooperation with other data protection authorities.
The target outcomes of our bilateral and multilateral engagements include
but are not limited to:
a. Knowledge exchange on Data Protection and Privacy
b. Mutual legal assistance on investigation of data breaches
c. Mutual legal assistance on enforcement of transborder decision
d. Mutual legal assistance on intergovernmental information sharing
In the last one year, the Commission participated in many international
meetings and knowledge exchange programmes involving experts and
regulators drawn from different jurisdictions.
The Commission gained invaluable knowledge through the capacity building
programmes organized by development partners, particularly from the World
Bank, European Investment Bank and French Development Agency through
the Nigeria Digital Identity Development Project Office (ID4D); the European
Union; GIZ; and Smart Africa.

5. REGULATORY ACTIONS
18
5.1 True Life Stories
(With modifications to some personal data in order to protect the privacy of
the affected data subjects).
“Oga, it is “Fi” for Female!”
Dooshima Kitama was a happy young lady until she was unable to make
calls through her phone. She was born a bouncy baby girl and she remained
so. However, someone changed her gender to male in error. She visited the
mobile network office to complain but she was informed that the problem
was with her National Identification Number. (NIN). She was sure she did
everything right on her NIN. After weeks of frantic troubleshooting, she
discovered that it was her Bank Verification Number (BVN) that affected
her NIN Data.
Dooshima felt her enemies were finally closing in. She remembered that
she got the BVN through her bank. “Something must have gone wrong in
the process of putting in her personal data”, she thought to herself and she
decided to go to the bank to complain. The customer care of her branch
could not help her. Her phone was not working. She could not access her
bank account. She could not get an international passport. All of these
needed valid NIN.
Dooshima thought all hope was lost. Going to court means her life will be
on hold until the court can resolve that she has a right to be treated as a
natural woman. She heard about the Commission and filed a complaint with
the Commission. The Commission investigated all the parties concerned.
The Bank for instance was invited from Lagos to a Pre-Action Conference. It
was discovered that the officer who inputted her data for BVN inputted “M”
for Female. The matter was resolved in favour of Dooshima, her gender was

Mr. Fred Fide was sleeping when he heard his wife shouting: “Haaa, Freeeeeedi!

without a radiator. He saw the picture and realized immediately that the loan
shark he had been battling to pay had finally made good on their threat to
embarrass him. “Abeg, abeg, na small loan I take, I no dey womanize. I will

19
Fred lodged a complaint with the Commission. The Commission invited the
online lender to a Pre-Action Conference through the active involvement of a
team of policemen working with the Commission. The firm denied operating
as a loan shark and the numbers used for carrying out the atrocious acts of
character assassination were disclaimed. The threat to Mr. Fred stopped

LESSONS LEARNT FROM REAL-LIFE CASES: -
• There should be an organizational mechanism for prompt resolution of
data subjects’ complaints.
• Data subjects should have the opportunity to properly verify their data
before submitting same.
• There should be a seamless interface between organizations for the
purposes of resolving data subjects’ complaints or addressing cross-
cutting requests.
• Loan Apps are overly intrusive. They generally violate the principles of
Data Protection and Privacy because they have access to contacts,
pictures, messages, etc. of data subjects.
• Organizations – particularly communication networks should be willing
to restrict or ban telephone lines that are implicated in privacy violations.
• There should be closer regulation of online lenders.
5.2 Systemic Remedies
Collaboration:- Under Joint Enforcement and Regulatory Taskforce, we are
collaborating with regulators to sanitize the digital lending space. For instance,
the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC)
requires lending companies to obtain data protection clearance from NDPC
before operation. The NDPC insists on full compliance with the NDPA in this
regard as each online lending company must carry out a comprehensive Data
Privacy Impact Assessment. Some of the regulators we are collaborating with
are:
• Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC)
• National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA)

Regulation:- The Commission drafted NDPA-GAID which addresses the

5.3 Systemic Impact
• Over 400 cases of privacy breaches involving shadowy loan sharks are
being addressed at the systemic level.
• Third party platforms being used for abuses are cooperating with
regulators in implementing deterrent measures. As at the 4th Quarter
of 2023, 203 loan Apps were approved under the JERTF, 38 received
conditional approval, 85 companies and Apps are under watch, and 47
were delisted.
• Regulators and security establishments are mainstreaming data
protection into their policies even at the design level. For instance, 2.5
million enrolees per month targeted under NIN will be registered under
a strengthened data protection regime.

NIGERIA & THE SHIFTING PARADIGM OF DATA
DIPLOMACY.
Ambassador Akinremi .A. Bolaji
- Director, Economic Trade and Investment Department, Ministry of Foreign Affairs
Since the advent of Convention 108 in 1981 and, lately,
the EU General Data Protection Regulation, 2018, the
paradigm of data diplomacy has been shifting at its very
tectonic plates. Gladly, Nigeria will not be caught in any
of its fault lines, thanks to the proactive steps the Federal
Government has taken in enacting the Nigeria Data
Protection Act as well as establishing an independent
Data Protection Authority; the Nigeria Data Protection
Commission (NDPC).
For the benefit of those who are just arriving at this new frontier of bilateral and
multilateral relations, it is important to explain the concept of data diplomacy.
Indeed, anyone who argues that data diplomacy was hardly a paramount
consideration before 2018 when the EU-GDPR came into force would be
right. However, such argument has become moot points in negotiations
on information sharing or movement of goods and services driven by data.
According to the scholarly article by Fatima Alfahim titled: “Data Diplomacy:
Turning bytes into Insights” (published by Blavanik School of Government,
Oxford University Voices):
Diplomacy has traditionally relied on backdoor channels of
communication and qualitative intelligence. But the rise in demand
for data-driven insights and technological innovation usher a new era
in which data becomes a strategic asset in our ever-changing world.
Data analysis could have a meaningful part to support core diplomatic
activities – negotiations, consular services, humanitarian response
and more. Trends and correlations could contribute to anticipatory
foreign policymaking.
When we bring this home to real bilateral relations, the importance of data
diplomacy is compelling. For instance, Nigeria is negotiating an agreement
with the United Kingdom in the general context of Migration and Justice (this
involves the management of their respective borders to enhance security
and combat transnational organized crime among others). In the era of data
protection, both countries are under obligation to negotiate data privacy and
protection for the agreement to move forward. This is also a grey area for the

Nigeria Data Protection Annual Report 2023
implementation of the Global Financial Action Task Force Recommendations
(involving Anti-Money Laundering/Counter-Financing Terrorism Systems).
Apart from security, we have also witnessed first-hand, the importance of data
31
in various bilateral consultation on trade and investment. Recently, various
agencies of government on the Nigeria Economic Trade and Investment
Forum have been interfacing with their counterparts from Netherlands,
Mexico, Cote d’Ivoire among others. In these meetings also data diplomacy
is playing a crucial role. The biggest selling point for Nigeria in terms of
Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability of data is that, we have statutory
reference point in the Nigeria Data Protection Act.
The growing currency of data diplomacy in Nigeria’s relations with the outside
world is a phenomenon that should be encouraged and supported. Thankfully,
the leaderships of our respective establishments have demonstrated
unwavering commitment in this regard. The Nigeria Economic Trade and
Investment Forum initiated by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs clearly illustrates
Nigeria’s commitment towards seamless information sharing- with due regard
for data diplomacy.
Before concluding, we must acknowledge the challenges of getting parties to
participate in meetings and agree diplomatically. This could be all the more
concerning in modern economies where technology has made the world one
sleepless market and prompt decisions are crucial. Thankfully, the diplomatic
community are mindful of these challenges.
Finally, it is also cheering to note that in the interactions with the Commission,
it also acknowledges the role of diplomacy in negotiating a sustainable data
governance system for the international community. The perspective of the
United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) remains the
reference point for the Commission on the way forward in the international
community. According to UNCTAD:
Data-driven digitalization creates global opportunities as well as
global challenges that require global solutions to harness the positive
and mitigate the negative impacts. Effective global governance
of data is a prerequisite for data to support the attainment of the
economic, social and environmental objectives of the 2030 Agenda
for Sustainable Development, with people at the centre. Efforts
to develop a global approach to the governance of data and cross-
border data flows should address a number of key policy areas and
priorities, including the following:
1. Developing a common understanding about definitions of key
data related concepts;
2. Establishing terms of access to data;

Nigeria Data Protection Annual Report 2023
3. Strengthening the measurement of the value of data and cross-
border data flows;
4. Dealing with data as a (global) public good;
32
5. Exploring emerging forms of data governance;
6. Agreeing on digital and data-related rights and principles;
7. Developing data-related standards; and increasing international
cooperation related to platform governance, including with regard
to competition policy and taxation in the digital economy.
What is evident from the foregoing is that Nigeria recognizes that the paradigm
of data diplomacy is shifting and that appropriate mechanisms are being put
in place to ensure that, we are well positioned to leverage the resulting data
flows for sustainable development.
